meta.title: Unterm — a terminal AI agents can control
meta.desc: The terminal AI agents can drive — now on its own high-performance kernel, 22ms from launch to a live MCP control surface. Live status for Claude Code / Codex / Gemini in every pane, an inbox for agents that need you, parallel fleets in isolated git worktrees, and diff-level review of everything they change. MCP + CLI, local-first, MIT.
cap.title: The complete control surface
cap.subtitle: Not a screenshot tour — the real surface every agent and script can call. 99 MCP methods across 21 namespaces, plus 32 CLI commands, all returning the same JSON.
cap.surfaces.note: Every method is reachable from MCP (JSON-RPC over TCP), the unterm-cli binary, the Web Settings HTTP API, and the GUI — one round-trip to meta.surface (or unterm-cli reference) returns this entire list live.
cap.cockpit.title: Agent Cockpit
cap.cockpit.body: See every CLI agent's live state (working / waiting / idle), jump to whichever one needs you from the Inbox, launch a fleet of N agents on one task in isolated git worktrees, and review, merge, or roll back what they produced — from the GUI, MCP, or CLI.
cap.session.title: Sessions & panes
cap.session.body: Spawn, split, focus, resize, and destroy panes from outside the terminal. Type into any pane character-by-character, read its cwd, poll until idle — no keystroke simulation.
cap.screen.title: Screen reading
cap.screen.body: Pull live viewport text, the full scrollback as one string, cursor position, or a regex search. detect_errors flags failed commands for an agent to react to.
cap.exec.title: Command execution
cap.exec.body: Run a command and stream output, run-and-wait for an exit code, send raw bytes, query status, cancel, or deliver a POSIX signal — structured results, not screen-scraping.
cap.agents.title: AI agent launcher
cap.agents.body: Install, authenticate, configure, and launch Claude Code / Codex / Gemini / OpenCode / Aider. The mcp-stdio bridge auto-wires each one back to this terminal's MCP server.
cap.identity.title: Identity profiles
cap.identity.body: Bind a window to a developer identity — GitHub PAT, AWS keys, npm token, SSH key, git author. Credentials live in the OS vault; 7 sniffers discover existing ones read-only.
cap.instance.title: Multi-instance
cap.instance.body: Each window is a NATO-named instance (alpha, bravo, charlie…). Enumerate every live Unterm on the machine, focus one, or retitle it — an agent routes work across windows by cwd or title.
cap.rec.title: Recording & replay
cap.rec.body: Record any session as an asciicast, replay it, or export to OSC-133 block-segmented markdown with token redaction — each block carries its command, output, exit code, and duration.
cap.capture.title: Capture & upload
cap.capture.body: Screenshot the screen, a window, or a drag-selected region; read the clipboard; or push a file to your own Aliyun OSS / Tencent COS / Qiniu bucket and get back a public URL — all over MCP.
cap.proxy.title: Proxy management
cap.proxy.body: Read the OS proxy state, switch between configured nodes, latency-test endpoints, or apply / clear system proxy overrides (macOS scutil · Windows registry · Linux env) — zero URL pasting.
cap.gov.title: Governance & audit
cap.gov.body: Every agent write is logged with its identity; a write-confirmation policy gates first contact. Test policy decisions, run the built-in self-test suite, and read liveness/readiness flags.
cap.workspace.title: Workspaces
cap.workspace.body: Save the current window's full pane / tab layout, list saved layouts, and restore one — an agent can snapshot a working set and bring it back later.
cap.meta.title: Self-describing surface
cap.meta.body: meta.surface returns every MCP method (with param schemas), every CLI subcommand, and every live keybinding in one call — so an agent that just connected learns the whole API without docs.

stand.subtitle: Three claims you can grep, build, or run yourself. No marketing fog.
stand.agents.title: The terminal you boot every AI coding CLI from
stand.agents.body: v0.18 makes Unterm a one-click launcher for Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, and Aider. Each agent's install command, OAuth flow, API key, and native config file are described by a signed manifest fetched from unterm.app; the runtime drops the key into your OS keychain, writes the agent's own JSON/TOML/YAML config (preserving unknown fields), exposes Unterm itself to the agent as an MCP server, and records the session into audit — all reachable from the CLI and the new AI Agents Web Settings tab.
stand.split.title: AI splits panes from outside the terminal
stand.split.body: session.split + session.focus over MCP let an external agent (Claude Code, Cursor, your script) carve the active window left / right / up / down and hand focus to the new pane — without simulating any keystroke. Built into the Python snippet on the hero. No other terminal exposes pane geometry to outside processes this way.
stand.audit.title: Every agent write is auditable, revocable, reviewable
stand.audit.body: Each session.input / exec.send is logged with the calling agent's identity. First write from a new agent triggers an Allow / Block / Always-allow banner. Trust persists to ~/.unterm/trusted_agents.json and is one click revocable from the Web Settings MCP tab. The status bar shows live MCP write count.
stand.identity.title: One window per developer identity
stand.identity.body: Bind a window to a coherent identity in one shot: GitHub PAT, AWS keys, npm token, OpenAI key, SSH key, git author. Credentials live in the OS-native vault (Keychain / Credential Manager / libsecret) — never on disk. Seven sniffers read existing credentials so first-time setup is empty.

tagline.title: AI controls the terminal. MCP makes it real.
tagline.body: Most terminals embed AI inside the binary. Unterm does the opposite: keep AI outside, expose the terminal as a surface that any external agent can grip via MCP. The terminal is the thing being controlled; the agent is the thing doing the work.
agents.title: Install every coding agent. One click each. No setup tax.
agents.subtitle: If you've ever tried to run more than one AI coding CLI side-by-side, you know the tax: npm install, OAuth flow, API key, ~/.config/<vendor>/<different format each>, env vars, profile separation. Unterm v0.18 collapses that into one settings tab + a CLI. No other terminal does this.
agents.card.install.title: Install in the GUI or via CLI
agents.card.install.body: Click Install on any agent card, or run unterm-cli agent install <id>. Unterm runs the right command for your platform (npm / pipx / etc.), verifies the binary lands on PATH, and re-detects automatically.
agents.card.auth.title: Official subscription first. BYO key stays opt-in.
agents.card.auth.body: Most agents ship with an official account or subscription login path (Claude Pro, ChatGPT Plus, Google AI Pro). Unterm defaults to that mode — no API key is ever silently injected. Switch to bring your own key or custom endpoint explicitly in the Configure form when you actually want per-token billing or a corporate gateway.
agents.card.signed.title: Ed25519-signed manifest catalog
agents.card.signed.body: The list of agents + their install commands isn't hard-coded into Unterm — it's a signed envelope served from unterm.app/api/agents/manifests. A compromise of the CDN can't push curl | sh to your machine; the public key is baked into every Unterm binary.
demo.title: One AI controls another AI through the terminal.

whatsnew.title: What's new in v0.61
whatsnew.perf54.title: 2.8× faster cold start, and no CPU spin under output floods
whatsnew.perf54.body: A performance release. Cold start ~780ms → ~280ms. Five startup-path wins: config keys validate against a precomputed set instead of rebuilding the whole config per key (Lua eval 297ms → 8ms), the redundant second config load is skipped, WSL distros are read from the registry instead of spawning wsl.exe, the 1119 built-in color schemes parse in parallel, and the GL context is prewarmed on a helper thread right after argument parsing. No more CPU core burned on output floods. On Windows, a throttled WM_PAINT handler used to leave the update region unvalidated, so the message loop spun at ~91% of a core during sustained output; it now drops to ~4%. MCP stays responsive mid-flood (was timing out at 30s, now answers in tens of milliseconds). Also fixed: the first terminal row no longer hides under the top bar, the settings-menu prewarm no longer fails on small glyph atlases, and unterm-cli without --id now targets the pane you're looking at.
whatsnew.composer53.title: Queue prompts for your agent, read Git at a glance
whatsnew.composer53.body: Driving agents, not just watching them. Composer — a prompt queue (Ctrl+Shift+J). Line up several prompts and run them into the active pane one after another; in auto-approve mode Composer smart-advances through an agent's confirmation prompts, so a batch of instructions runs to completion without babysitting each step. Read-only Git panel (Ctrl+Shift+G). A right-docked panel shows the active pane's branch, upstream tracking, and working-tree status at a glance — the terminal reflows around it and it toggles away just as fast. Sidebar tabs read as their work. Each row is now labeled from its foreground command, and the top bar, sidebar, and bottom status bar share one unified frame. Steadier startup. Fixed a Windows crash on GPU-less / old-GPU machines where the WebGpu fallback could abort the process before the window appeared.
whatsnew.agents52.title: More agents out of the box, smoother frames, and steadier Windows
whatsnew.agents52.body: Agent coverage and stability. Two more agents recognized on first launch. The baked manifest now ships Kimi Code CLI (Moonshot login or bring-your-own key) and Trae Agent (provider / model / config-driven), so they're auto-discovered and registerable like the rest without waiting for a manifest refresh. Fewer GUI stalls. The left tab bar, status bar, top stats strip, ghost-text, and pane paint paths were reworked to cut per-frame work, so the window stays responsive under load. Steadier on Windows. A window can no longer be shrunk to a size too small to drag back open, and copy/paste now retries when another process briefly holds the clipboard instead of failing outright.
whatsnew.native51.title: Native macOS text weight, a roomier sidebar, and a tab list that scales
whatsnew.native51.body: Typography and chrome polish. Native glyph weight. The CoreText rasterizer now applies the system's grayscale font smoothing by default, so terminal and chrome text pick up the same stem-darkening as Terminal.app instead of rendering thin — the new font_smoothing option (default on) lets you switch to the lighter Warp-style HiDPI look. Roomier left sidebar. Larger UI type and looser row leading, a single quiet footer link, and a generous gap above the add-tab + so it's no longer mis-clicked. Scales to many sessions. Per-tab metadata is gathered only for the visible rows, so a window with dozens of tabs stays responsive. Plus the split divider now draws cleanly to the window edge and the per-pane close button sits in the pane's corner.
whatsnew.chrome44.title: Warp-style chrome — unified top bar, left tab sidebar, per-pane stats
whatsnew.chrome44.body: The chrome got rebuilt around three changes that ship together. (1) Unified top bar. The split gray-titlebar-above / dark-tab-row-below collapses into one panel that tracks palette.background; traffic lights drop into the tab row and the chrome height matches Warp's rhythm. Quick-action icons (palette, tree sidebar, split, dir-jump, search, settings) are Codicons rendered through the bundled SymbolsNerdFontMono so they're vector-crisp on every platform. (2) Left vertical tab bar (tab_bar_position = "Left") — tabs become rows with a agent · directory subtitle (which MCP agent is currently driving that pane), drag to reorder, double-click to rename, and a pinned footer linking back to doaipm.com. (3) Per-pane stats strip rides on the right side of the top bar: git branch + dirty/ahead/behind, the foreground process's CPU / RSS / uptime, and the active AI agent when one is attached — all refreshed off the render thread so typing is never slowed. Workspace restore now reopens every tab at its previous cwd instead of one fresh shell, and per-binary save state means Unterm.app and a dev build don't trample each other.
whatsnew.unitop.title: A unified window top — the gray title bar is gone
whatsnew.unitop.body: macOS used to draw a gray native title bar above Unterm's tab strip — a cold band that clashed with the dark terminal below. v0.39 collapses the top into a single strip the same color as your content: the traffic-light buttons sit in the tab row, the separate title bar is gone, and the whole top follows your active theme's background automatically — any theme, light or dark, stays seamless. Fixes the macOS path where the integrated title buttons were being silently disabled (the title-button style now resolves per-platform), so the window finally reads as one piece instead of three clashing bands.
whatsnew.uipolish.title: A more polished look out of the box + a new logo
whatsnew.uipolish.body: v0.38 is a visual pass on the defaults. Content gets room to breathe (window padding 4px → 16/16/10/8), the bundled JetBrains Mono with ligatures is now the default font (no more falling back to whatever monospace the system happens to have), line-height opens up to 1.15, and the warm Notion Dark scheme is the default on fresh installs — window chrome and the tab bar are warmed to the same palette so nothing clashes. The app icon is redesigned too: a warm-black monogram where a teal U cradles an amber T over a terminal block cursor. Deeper polish — active-pane treatment, status-bar grouping, a tasteful default prompt — is queued for the next round.
whatsnew.rotationfix.title: Auto-rotation that never drops your network
whatsnew.rotationfix.body: Proxy auto-rotation used to fail over on a single slow health check — one jittery probe and your exit node got yanked out mid-connection, dropping logged-in sessions, long downloads, and SSH. v0.37 makes failover deliberate: the active node is retried within each check and must miss two consecutive checks before Unterm switches; the health-probe timeout widens to 5s and the minimum interval to 10s. A transient hiccup no longer rotates the whole system's proxy out from under your terminal — rotation fires only when a node is genuinely dead. It honors the rule that has governed proxy support from day one: the proxy must never break the terminal. Drive it from the Web Settings rotation pool or unterm-cli proxy rotation.
whatsnew.aicomplete.title: Type any AI CLI flag — Unterm finishes it inline
whatsnew.aicomplete.body: Building on the per-CLI flag catalog, v0.34 brings full flag and argument ghost-text completion for the AI coding CLIs. Start typing claude --, codex --, gemini --, opencode --, or aider -- in any pane and Unterm completes the flag name inline — and where the flag takes a known value (model names, approval modes, sandbox levels) it predicts the argument too — as grey ghost text. → / Tab accepts. The completions come from the same signed manifest catalog that drives the Launch-options checkboxes, so the inline predictor and the GUI never drift apart.
whatsnew.winclash.title: Zero-config Clash detection on Windows
whatsnew.winclash.body: Proxy rotation reads your Clash / mihomo nodes through the controller API — but Windows has no Unix socket, so v0.33 auto-discovers the TCP external-controller address + secret from the usual Clash Verge / mihomo config locations under %APPDATA% / %LOCALAPPDATA%. Rotation now works out of the box on Windows exactly as it does on macOS and Linux. Also in v0.33: turning rotation on now switches the proxy on if it was off (no more silently-armed-but-idle rotation), and AI-CLI command-name completion joins the flag/argument ghost text.
whatsnew.launchflags.title: Pick an AI CLI's flags — Unterm autocompletes them
whatsnew.launchflags.body: Each AI coding CLI has dozens of launch flags (model, sandbox, approval-mode, skip-trust, yolo, …) and remembering the names is friction. v0.23 ships a per-CLI flag catalog in the manifest — 22 flags across Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, and Aider, each with an i18n label, a description, and a risk tag (safe / caution / danger). The catalog drives three surfaces from one source: Web Settings → AI Agents → Launch options renders the catalog as risk-colored checkboxes (⚠ on auto-approve flags; never pre-checked); the saved selection composes into the launch command for both the GUI and unterm-cli agent launch; and when you type gemini -- in any pane, Unterm's ghost-text predictor completes the flag name inline (→ / Tab accepts). The aggressive --yolo / --dangerously-skip-permissions family is exposed as opt-in only, so the audit design isn't undermined by a forced default. Also in v0.23: agent install now works from the Dock-launched Unterm on macOS (resolves npm/pipx via Homebrew, npm-global, nvm/fnm, …) and on Windows (npm.cmd shim invocation); the unterm-cli reference CLI registry is resynced to the real clap surface (theme switch, lang current, full profile / agent / proxy subcommands); selftest.run no longer false-fails on macOS/Linux; and the live unterm.app/api/agents/manifests envelope was republished so the v0.22 autowire fix (.mcp.json path, Gemini autowire) finally reaches online users.
whatsnew.clashrotate.title: Proxy rotation that reads your nodes — you just tick the boxes
whatsnew.clashrotate.body: v0.30 shipped endpoint-level rotation; v0.31 makes it actually useful. Unterm now talks to your proxy software's Clash / mihomo controller (over its Unix socket or TCP API — Clash, Clash Verge, ClashX, mihomo, sing-box), reads your real node groups and nodes with live latency + reachability, and lets you tick which ones to rotate among — no hand-typing endpoint URLs. When the active node stops responding, Unterm delay-tests the pool and switches the group to the fastest live pick, all through the controller API. Non-Clash setups fall back to manual endpoint nodes. Also in v0.31: the scrollbar now follows the active pane in a split — it sits on whichever pane has focus, instead of always pinning to the window edge.
whatsnew.rotation.title: Proxy auto-rotation — and a terminal that never silently loses the network
whatsnew.rotation.body: v0.30 adds endpoint-level proxy auto-rotation: pick a pool of nodes in the proxy panel and Unterm health-checks the active one, failing over to the fastest reachable node the moment it dies. It's software-agnostic — endpoint-level failover, so it works with any Clash / V2Ray / sing-box setup and survives you switching proxy apps. Just as important, proxy injection is now liveness-probed before it touches a shell: if the configured proxy port isn't accepting connections, Unterm injects nothing and the terminal stays on a direct connection instead of routing every command into a black hole — a dead proxy can no longer look like "my VPN broke". Drive it all from the Web Settings pool checkboxes or unterm-cli proxy rotation. Also in v0.30: a clean window-edge scrollbar (on by default, themed thumb), the warm Notion-Dark theme across the whole app and website, and a roomier settings menu.
whatsnew.autodiscovery.title: Every AI agent on your machine auto-discovers Unterm — now native on ARM too
whatsnew.autodiscovery.body: v0.22 wired up agents that Unterm launches. v0.24 closes the other half: on first launch (per version) Unterm registers its unterm MCP server into every AI coding agent installed on the machine — Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Windsurf, OpenCode — by merging into each one's global config (never clobbering; an existing-but-unparseable config is refused, not overwritten) and dropping a short marker-delimited note into their CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md / GEMINI.md. So even an agent you started in some other terminal knows Unterm is here and can drive it. The mcp-stdio bridge self-discovers the live instance, so a static registration keeps working across restarts and multi-window. Run unterm-cli setup-ai any time to re-sync, --remove to undo; connected agents also get a usage brief via the MCP initialize instructions field. Also in v0.24: native ARM64 builds. Unterm now ships five targets — macOS, Windows x64 + arm64, Linux x64 + arm64 — each built natively in CI on its own architecture, with arm64 ConPTY + ANGLE bundled for Windows-on-ARM.
whatsnew.autowire.title: Agents auto-wire to Unterm's MCP on launch
whatsnew.autowire.body: Launch Claude Code / Codex / Gemini / OpenCode from Unterm and they come pre-connected to this terminal's MCP server — no manual config. A new unterm-cli mcp-stdio bridge speaks the MCP stdio protocol and proxies every call to the running instance's control server, so the launcher can write each agent's native MCP config (.mcp.json for Claude Code, ~/.codex/config.toml for Codex, ~/.gemini/settings.json for Gemini, opencode.json for OpenCode — each in its own correct schema, merged not clobbered) pointing at the bridge. The agent can drive the terminal it lives in from its first prompt. Also in v0.22: split-focus is now shown by a thin accent bar on the active pane (no more harsh frame), the per-pane scrollbar no longer bleeds into the status bar, and the Notion Light / Notion Dark themes finally show + apply correctly from Web Settings.
whatsnew.reference.title: One MCP call now returns every method, every CLI, every shortcut
whatsnew.reference.body: A new meta.surface MCP method + unterm-cli reference + a Reference tab in Web Settings — same JSON behind all three. An agent that just connected gets the full surface (60+ MCP methods with param schemas, 22 CLI subcommands, every currently-bound keybinding read live from your unterm.lua) in one round trip; users can search it locally without leaving Settings. The MCP method list is now the source of truth for both server.capabilities and dispatch — adding a new method requires updating one registry, no more drift between dispatch and the published catalog. unterm-cli reference --section keys --filter copy for a quick local cheatsheet; --section mcp / cli for the others.
whatsnew.agentdump.title: Two more ways to hand a pane to an AI
whatsnew.agentdump.body: Two paired pieces that close the agent-handoff loop without dragging files around. (1) screen.scrollback_text MCP + unterm-cli scrollback dump the full pane history + viewport as a single string — strictly better than a rendered "long screenshot" for LLM hand-off: parses natively, no OCR, no font fidelity loss, optional ANSI escapes for color-aware analysis. (2) upload.file MCP + unterm-cli upload <file> push a local file to your own Aliyun OSS / Tencent COS / Qiniu Kodo bucket and return a public URL. Credentials live in ~/.unterm/upload.json and never leave the box — signing is hand-rolled HMAC-SHA1 so we don't drag in any vendor SDK. Together with capture.window, an agent can screenshot → upload → embed the URL in one round trip. Plus: new Notion Light / Notion Dark / Classic Dark color schemes with an active-pane outline that survives split focus, and a Windows fix that clears a stuck SPI_SETSCREENREADER flag so PSReadLine and bracketed paste keep working when another app forgets to reset it.
whatsnew.windowtitle.title: Window titles lead with project name
whatsnew.windowtitle.body: Open three Unterm windows for three projects and the Dock / Cmd-Tab / Mission Control window-list used to show Unterm — alpha — zsh for all of them — same prefix, indistinguishable. v0.19 flips to Apple's <Document> — <App> convention and leads with the project directory basename: unterm — Unterm (alpha), solomd — Unterm (bravo). The NATO instance id moves to a trailing parenthesis so screenshot-OCR agents still get the mapping back to ~/.unterm/instances/<id>.json. Explicit user overrides (set via unterm-cli instance set-title or MCP) still take priority.
whatsnew.subtitle: Proxy auto-rotation that survives flaky nodes, full ghost-text completion for every AI CLI's flags and arguments, and zero-config Clash detection on Windows — the most recent releases, in four cards.
whatsnew.agents.title: AI Agent integration: 5 first-party CLIs, one click each
whatsnew.agents.body: Install / authenticate / configure / launch any of Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, or Aider directly from Unterm's Web Settings or `unterm-cli agent ...`. Each agent is described by a signed manifest (Ed25519, served from unterm.app/api/agents/manifests, with a baked fallback so offline installs still work). Settings are schema-driven: edit them in a typed form and Unterm writes the agent's native config file with `preserve_unknown_keys` semantics; API keys land in the OS keychain via the existing identity profile. New Shell → AI Agents menu spawns each one in a fresh tab with the right env injected. Every launched session lands in the audit index tagged agent_id / manifest_version / profile.
whatsnew.reflexive.title: session.split + session.focus + an MCP trust panel
whatsnew.reflexive.body: Three pieces that close the loop on "AI drives the terminal — including its own." session.split lets an agent split a pane left/right/up/down without simulating a keystroke; session.focus makes the new pane active so the hand-off is visible to the user. Both are exercised in the live snippet above. Web Settings gains a new MCP tab: a runtime trust list (with per-agent write counts and one-click revoke) plus the last 80 audited write attempts in a sortable table. Trust persists to ~/.unterm/trusted_agents.json so Alt+A survives a restart. New /docs/agent-recipes page collects 9 copy-pastable Python snippets.
whatsnew.aiterminal.title: Agent-aware terminal — audit, suggest, ghost text
whatsnew.aiterminal.body: Three pieces fall into place to make Unterm a real AI-collaboration terminal. (1) Every session.input / exec.send is audited; the first time a new agent writes to a pane, a blocking banner asks the user — [Enter] allow, [Esc] block, [Alt+A] always-allow. The new mcp:N chip in the status bar tracks cumulative MCP PTY writes; click to copy the audit log. (2) session.suggest lets agents propose text without ever touching the PTY directly — a ✨ suggest bar sits above the status bar, [Tab] accepts, [Esc] dismisses, [Alt+Enter] accepts and runs. (3) Fish-style grey ghost text continues your input from cross-pane shell history; [→] / [End] accepts the prediction. All three keystrokes (Tab, Esc, Enter) pass through to the shell when no banner / suggestion / prediction is showing — vim, less, fzf all keep working unchanged.
whatsnew.configfix.title: Config resilience — unknown fields no longer crash
whatsnew.configfix.body: Setting an unrecognized key in your unterm.lua (e.g. a future or experimental option) used to abort the process on Windows release builds. The Lua FFI callback crossed a panic = abort boundary and triggered an unrecoverable crash with no diagnostic. v0.15 defaults config_builder() to non-strict mode: unknown fields produce a visible warning and the app continues to start normally.
whatsnew.profiles.title: Identity profiles — one window per identity
whatsnew.profiles.body: Bind a window to a coherent developer identity in one shot: GitHub PAT, AWS keys, npm token, OpenAI key, git author, SSH key routing. Tokens live in the OS-native vault (Keychain / Credential Manager / libsecret), never in ~/.unterm/. Seven sniffers (gh / aws / npm / ssh / docker / gcloud / netrc) discover existing credentials read-only. CLI + read-only MCP namespace expose the system to agents that need to know which identity is running. New chip in the status bar tells you at a glance — click to spawn a new window in the next profile.
whatsnew.flash.title: Sync pre-show paint kills the Windows white flash
whatsnew.flash.body: Three iterations to root-cause it: the DWM samples its redirection bitmap before WM_ERASEBKGND fires, so any fix routed through the message pump arrives too late. v0.12 renders one synchronous frame of real terminal content into the backbuffer in wezterm-gui before window.show(). Spawn-to-visible is ~880ms, no flash. Linux/macOS paths unchanged — the new path is cfg(windows) gated.
whatsnew.instances.title: Multi-instance NATO names
whatsnew.instances.body: Each Unterm process owns one instance with a NATO-phonetic name (alpha, bravo, charlie…). MCP instance.list enumerates all live instances; agents pick by cwd, title, or start order. Window title becomes Unterm — alpha — Project for visual mapping.
whatsnew.utf8.title: Auto UTF-8 on Windows
whatsnew.utf8.body: PowerShell and cmd.exe spawned by Unterm get UTF-8 output by default — no more mojibake on zh-CN, ja-JP, ko-KR Windows installs. Agents don't have to fix the user's $PROFILE; we wrap at spawn time with chcp 65001 + Console.OutputEncoding setup.
whatsnew.cwd.title: CWD in the status bar
whatsnew.cwd.body: Active pane's working directory shows up between the shell name and dimensions, with $HOME → ~ and middle truncation. Click to copy the full path. Works across local panes, mux clients, and SSH-forwarded sessions.
principles.title: Six principles, no exceptions
principles.local.title: Local-first, no cloud
principles.local.body: Every server, every API endpoint, every recording lives on 127.0.0.1. No login, no telemetry, no subscription. Your shell history is yours.
principles.outside.title: AI lives outside the terminal
principles.outside.body: No chat overlay, no ghost-text autocomplete, no inline AI panel. The terminal is the surface — Claude Code, Cursor, your scripts grip it through MCP.
principles.mcp.title: MCP is a first-class surface
principles.mcp.body: Every product feature ships with an MCP method and a CLI subcommand on day one. If it can't be driven from outside, it doesn't ship.
principles.parity.title: Cross-platform parity is correctness
principles.parity.body: A feature that works on Windows but bails on macOS or Linux is a bug, not a 'not yet supported.' Mac, Linux, Windows ship together.
principles.subtraction.title: Subtraction over decoration
principles.subtraction.body: When a feature belongs to the OS, use the OS. Keep AI generation outside the terminal, keep core operation local, and use native Finder integration on macOS.
principles.subscription.title: Respect the subscription. Default OAuth.
principles.subscription.body: When you install an AI agent through Unterm, the default authentication mode is the vendor's official subscription (OAuth) — your Pro / Plus / Team plan. We never silently inject an API key into a session; per-token billing happens only if you explicitly switch the auth mode to 'bring your own API key' or 'custom endpoint' in the Configure form. This is an opt-in, not a footgun.
cmp.title: Unterm vs. a native terminal vs. a paid AI terminal
cmp.subtitle: The native terminal (Terminal.app) is the baseline you already have. Warp is the paid AI terminal. iTerm2 and Ghostty are the free power terminals. Unterm sits in its own lane: everything an external agent can grip from outside.
cmp.r.autowire: Agents auto-wire to the terminal's MCP
cmp.legend: ✓ yes · ✗ no · ~ partial · ×N count. The ✗ by design on "AI inside" is the whole thesis: Unterm keeps the AI outside and exposes the terminal as the surface it grips.
cmp.note: Reflects publicly documented features as of 2026-05. Warp is closed-source with a cloud-backed free tier + paid Team/Pro plans; iTerm2 ships a Python scripting API and an opt-in AI command plugin; Ghostty has no Windows build yet. Corrections welcome on GitHub.

cmp.c.wezterm.title: Unterm vs WezTerm: former fork, now its own kernel — plus an agent layer
cmp.c.wezterm.desc: Unterm began as a WezTerm fork; since v0.61 it runs on its own next-core kernel and adds an MCP server, a scripting CLI, and one-click AI-agent install so agents can drive the terminal. Feature-by-feature comparison.
cmp.c.wezterm.tagline: Unterm started as a fork of WezTerm's renderer and mux — since v0.61 it runs on its own next-core kernel, wrapped in an agent-control surface WezTerm doesn't ship.
cmp.c.wezterm.intro: WezTerm is an excellent, mature GPU terminal: Lua config, a battle-tested multiplexer, SSH domains, and cross-platform builds, all MIT-licensed. Unterm started as a fork of that foundation to answer a different question — how does an AI agent operate a terminal? — by exposing the whole app over MCP and a CLI. Since v0.61 the fork is gone: Unterm runs on its own next-core kernel (~12k lines, 10 direct dependencies), with only portable-pty and termwiz's Unicode tables remaining from the WezTerm ecosystem.
cmp.c.wezterm.a1: An MCP server built in. Any LLM agent can list/create/split panes, run commands, read the screen and scrollback, and capture screenshots — WezTerm has a control CLI for panes, but nothing an external agent speaks natively.
cmp.c.wezterm.a2: One-click AI agents + auto-wiring. Install and sign in to Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, or Aider in a click, and Unterm registers itself into each client's global MCP config automatically.
cmp.c.wezterm.a3: Agent-workflow surface. Identity profiles (per-window secrets from the OS keychain), multi-instance windows, redacted Markdown session recording, scrollback capture, and probe-gated proxy — none of which live in stock WezTerm.
cmp.c.wezterm.win: WezTerm is the mature project with a deeper, more configurable terminal surface (Lua scripting, extensive keybinding and multiplexer features) and a longer track record. If you don't want any AI/agent layer, WezTerm is the leaner, more customizable pure terminal.
cmp.c.wezterm.verdict: Want a fast, scriptable general-purpose terminal? WezTerm is a strong choice. Want a native terminal kernel designed together with authenticated agent control, Cockpit, Review, profiles, proxy identity, and reversible workflows? That is what Unterm now builds as one product.
cmp.c.warp.title: Unterm vs Warp: the open-source, local, no-login alternative
cmp.c.warp.desc: Warp is a polished but closed-source, cloud-backed AI terminal that needs an account. Unterm is MIT-licensed, fully local, free, and built for agents to drive via MCP. Side-by-side comparison.
cmp.c.warp.tagline: Both put AI in the terminal — but Warp bakes in a cloud assistant behind a login, while Unterm stays open-source, local, and agent-driven.
cmp.c.warp.intro: Warp is a genuinely slick AI terminal: command blocks, inline AI suggestions, and team features. The trade-offs are that it's closed-source, requires an account/login, and routes AI through the cloud. Unterm takes the opposite stance — the AI lives outside the terminal, and the terminal exposes itself so your agent can operate it.
cmp.c.warp.a1: Open source & local. MIT-licensed, runs entirely on your machine, no account and no login — nothing about your session leaves the box unless you send it.
cmp.c.warp.a2: Bring your own agent. Instead of one built-in cloud assistant, Unterm installs and drives Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, or Aider — and exposes itself over MCP so any of them can run commands and read the screen.
cmp.c.warp.a3: Free, forever, cross-platform. No freemium tiers or seat pricing; macOS, Linux, and Windows; a scripting CLI and identity profiles for real automation.
cmp.c.warp.win: Warp's built-in AI UX is more turnkey — command blocks, inline autocomplete, and a cloud assistant that works the moment you sign in, plus polished team/collaboration features. If you want an AI terminal that just works out of the box and don't mind the account, cloud, and closed source, Warp is the smoother ready-made experience.
cmp.c.warp.verdict: If you want a hosted AI assistant baked into the terminal and are fine with login + closed source, Warp is excellent. If you want an open-source, local, no-login terminal that your coding agent drives — and to keep the AI outside — Unterm is the alternative built for exactly that.
cmp.c.wave-terminal.title: Unterm vs Wave Terminal: agent-driven vs AI-widget
cmp.c.wave-terminal.desc: Wave is an open-source terminal with a block-based UI and an AI chat widget. Unterm exposes itself over MCP so agents drive the terminal, and installs coding agents in one click. Feature comparison.
cmp.c.wave-terminal.tagline: Wave adds an AI chat widget next to the terminal; Unterm turns the terminal itself into something an agent can operate.
cmp.c.wave-terminal.intro: Wave Terminal is a strong open-source (Apache-2.0) terminal: a flexible block/drag-drop workspace, inline file previews and editing, durable SSH sessions, and an AI chat widget that works with your own keys or local models. Unterm shares the open-source, local, BYO-key stance but is built around a different idea — the terminal as a surface an external agent grips, not a chat panel beside it.
cmp.c.wave-terminal.a1: MCP-native, not a side widget. Agents drive panes, commands, screen reads, and captures through Unterm's MCP server + CLI — automatable and headless, beyond an interactive chat box.
cmp.c.wave-terminal.a2: One-click coding agents. Install and sign into Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, or Aider, auto-wired into their MCP configs — rather than a single built-in assistant.
cmp.c.wave-terminal.a3: Agent-ops built in. Identity profiles, multi-instance windows, redacted Markdown recording, and proxy rotation — the plumbing for running agents, not just chatting with one.
cmp.c.wave-terminal.win: Wave is the richer interactive workspace: drag-and-drop blocks, inline file preview and editing, a built-in graphical editor, web widgets, and durable SSH sessions that survive disconnects. If you want an all-in-one graphical terminal workspace to work in by hand, Wave packs in more.
cmp.c.wave-terminal.verdict: Want an AI chat widget and a block-based workspace to drive yourself? Wave is great. Want a terminal your agent operates end-to-end — install, run, read, capture — over a real MCP surface? That's Unterm's focus.
cmp.c.terax.title: Unterm vs Terax: an MCP-driveable terminal vs a bundled agent IDE
cmp.c.terax.desc: Terax is a tiny Tauri AI terminal with a built-in editor and multi-agent side-panel. Unterm exposes itself over MCP so any external agent drives it, and installs coding agents in one click. Comparison.
cmp.c.terax.tagline: Both are AI-native terminals — Terax bundles its own agent IDE; Unterm lets any external agent drive the terminal over MCP.
cmp.c.terax.intro: Terax is an impressive, tiny (~7 MB) Tauri terminal with a built-in code editor, a git graph, a web preview pane, and a multi-agent AI side-panel using your own keys or local models. Unterm shares the open-source, AI-native, BYO stance but draws the line differently — instead of bundling an agent, it exposes the terminal over MCP so the agents you already use can operate it, and renders natively rather than in a webview.
cmp.c.terax.a1: Drive-any-agent, not one bundled agent. Unterm's MCP server + CLI let Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, and others list panes, run commands, and read the screen — you keep your agent of choice.
cmp.c.terax.a2: One-click install + auto-wiring. Set up and sign into the major coding agents in a click, and Unterm registers itself into each one's global MCP config.
cmp.c.terax.a3: Native terminal, agent-ops built in. A native (non-web) renderer plus identity profiles, multi-instance, session recording, screen capture, and proxy — the surface for running agents, not an editor bundled in.
cmp.c.terax.win: Terax packs more into one app: a real code editor, a git graph, a web-preview pane, and a built-in multi-agent workflow — all in a ~7 MB download, with an Android build too. If you want an all-in-one AI coding IDE that happens to live in a terminal, Terax bundles more out of the box.
cmp.c.terax.verdict: Want a bundled editor + agent IDE in one tiny app? Terax is a great pick. Want a terminal that the external coding agents you already run can drive over MCP, natively rendered? That's Unterm.
cmp.c.iterm2.title: Unterm vs iTerm2: cross-platform, agent-native vs the macOS power terminal
cmp.c.iterm2.desc: iTerm2 is the mature macOS power terminal with a Python API. Unterm is cross-platform, exposes an MCP server for agents, and installs AI coding agents in one click. Feature-by-feature comparison.
cmp.c.iterm2.tagline: iTerm2 is the definitive macOS power terminal; Unterm is cross-platform and built for AI agents to drive.
cmp.c.iterm2.intro: iTerm2 is a superb, deeply mature macOS terminal — triggers, profiles, a Python scripting API, and years of polish. Its constraints are that it's macOS-only and its automation is a Python API rather than an agent-native surface. Unterm runs on macOS, Linux, and Windows and is built around MCP so LLM agents operate it directly.
cmp.c.iterm2.a1: Cross-platform. The same agent-driveable terminal on macOS, Linux, and Windows — iTerm2 is macOS-only.
cmp.c.iterm2.a2: MCP + one-click agents. An MCP server any LLM speaks, a scripting CLI, and one-click install of Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, and Aider auto-wired into their configs.
cmp.c.iterm2.a3: Agent-workflow features. Identity profiles, multi-instance windows, redacted Markdown recording, screen capture, and proxy rotation — aimed at running agents, not just interactive use.
cmp.c.iterm2.win: On macOS, iTerm2 is hard to beat for interactive power use: an enormous, refined feature set, triggers, and a mature Python API, honed over many years. If you're macOS-only and want the deepest hand-driven terminal, iTerm2 is the gold standard.
cmp.c.iterm2.verdict: macOS-only and want the most mature interactive terminal? iTerm2. Want one agent-native terminal across mac, Linux, and Windows that your AI agents drive over MCP? Unterm is built for that.
cmp.c.ghostty.title: Unterm vs Ghostty: a fast terminal vs an agent-driveable one
cmp.c.ghostty.desc: Ghostty is a fast, minimal native GPU terminal for macOS and Linux. Unterm adds an MCP server, a CLI, and one-click AI agents, and runs on Windows too. Side-by-side comparison.
cmp.c.ghostty.tagline: Ghostty is a lean, fast, native terminal; Unterm adds the agent-control layer and Windows support.
cmp.c.ghostty.intro: Ghostty is a fantastic, fast native GPU terminal (built in Zig, MIT-licensed) with great defaults for macOS and Linux. It's deliberately minimal and has no AI/agent story. Unterm is also a GPU terminal, but its whole point is the layer on top — an MCP server and CLI that let agents drive it — and it ships on Windows as well.
cmp.c.ghostty.a1: Agents can drive it. A built-in MCP server + scripting CLI let LLM agents run commands, read the screen, and capture output — Ghostty has none of this by design.
cmp.c.ghostty.a2: One-click AI agents. Install and sign into Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, or Aider in a click, auto-wired into their MCP configs.
cmp.c.ghostty.a3: Windows + agent-ops. Runs on macOS, Linux, and Windows, plus identity profiles, multi-instance, session recording, and proxy — Ghostty is mac+Linux only.
cmp.c.ghostty.win: Ghostty is leaner and, for a pure terminal, blazing fast with beautiful defaults and a tiny footprint. If you want the most minimal, high-performance terminal on macOS or Linux and have no interest in an AI/agent layer, Ghostty is a superb choice.
cmp.c.ghostty.verdict: Want the leanest, fastest pure terminal on mac/Linux? Ghostty is excellent. Want a GPU terminal that AI agents can actually operate — and that also runs on Windows? That's what Unterm adds.

mouse.title: Right-click is copy & paste, not a menu
mouse.subtitle: The whole copy-paste loop lives on one button. With text selected, right-click copies and clears the selection; with nothing selected, the same click pastes at the cursor. No context menu ever opens, nothing to dismiss — one hand on the mouse reads output on one pane and feeds it to the next.
mouse.copy.title: Select, click — copied
mouse.copy.body: Drag across output, or just double-click a word. Right-click: it's on the clipboard and the highlight clears itself, so the pane is instantly ready for the next gesture.
mouse.paste.title: Click again — pasted
mouse.paste.body: No selection? The same right-click pastes at the prompt. Copy from one pane, click into another, click again — command moved, zero keystrokes. An empty clipboard is a quiet no-op, never an error.
mouse.ctrl.title: Ctrl+click, the macOS way
mouse.ctrl.body: macOS treats Ctrl+click as a secondary click, and so does Unterm — trackpad, Magic Mouse, or any third-party driver. Only a bare Ctrl qualifies, so your own Ctrl-combo mouse bindings and the Ctrl+Shift window drag stay untouched. Inside mouse-aware TUIs like vim or Claude Code, a Shift+drag selection completes with a plain right-click copy; without a selection the app keeps its own right-click (hold Shift to force a paste).
mouse.note: Live-verified end-to-end on macOS in v0.57.1 — copy, paste, Ctrl+click, and the empty-clipboard no-op, all through real mouse events.
faq.mouse.q: How do I copy and paste with just the mouse?
faq.mouse.a: Right-click does both: with a selection it copies (and clears the highlight); without one it pastes at the cursor. On macOS, Ctrl+click is the same gesture. Inside terminal apps that take over the mouse (vim, htop, Claude Code), select with Shift+drag and a plain right-click still copies; without a selection the app keeps its own right-click — hold Shift to force Unterm's paste. There is no context menu to dismiss, and an empty clipboard is a quiet no-op.
faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.what.a: A cross-platform terminal emulator with built-in MCP, HTTP, and CLI control surfaces. The product thesis: terminal as MCP-controllable surface, so any external AI agent can drive it from outside instead of having an AI baked into the terminal itself.
faq.mcp.q: How does it work with Claude Code, Cursor, or other agents?
faq.mcp.a: Each Unterm window starts a local MCP server (TCP, JSON-RPC, auth-token gated). Point your MCP client at 127.0.0.1:<port> — the port + token are written to ~/.unterm/server.json on launch. The agent can spawn shells, run commands, read pane state, capture screenshots, toggle recording, and switch settings.
faq.multi.q: How do I drive multiple Unterm windows from one agent?
faq.multi.a: Each Unterm process is one instance with a NATO-phonetic name (alpha, bravo, …) recorded in ~/.unterm/instances/<name>.json. Call instance.list on any one of them to enumerate; pick by cwd / title / start order; connect to that instance's port with its auth token. ~/.unterm/active.json points at the most recent live instance for single-instance fallbacks.
faq.warp.q: How is this different from Warp?
faq.warp.a: Warp embeds AI inside a closed cloud orchestrator (Oz) — external tools like Claude Code can't drive Warp from outside. Unterm picks the third lane: keep AI out of the terminal, expose the terminal itself as an MCP-controllable surface, and let any agent grip it. No cloud, no login.
faq.privacy.a: Nowhere external. MCP and Web Settings servers bind to 127.0.0.1 only. Session recordings land under <project>/.unterm/sessions/ with built-in redaction for tokens. There is no telemetry, no analytics, no login, no cloud round-trip. Your shell history is yours.
faq.telemetry.q: Does Unterm phone home, even once?
faq.telemetry.a: No. Zero telemetry by default — not even an opt-in dialog. The only outbound HTTP requests Unterm makes are: (1) at user request, when you click a download link in Web Settings; (2) by your shell, like normal — anything your terminal would do, it still does. We don't ship analytics, error reporting, install pings, or update checks.
faq.cost.q: Is there a paid tier or premium feature?
faq.cost.a: No. Unterm is MIT-licensed; the same single binary ships every feature. No subscription, no Pro tier, no plugin marketplace, no "buy now to unlock split panes." If you'd like to support the project, the Sponsor section above is the only ask.
faq.size.q: How big is the install and runtime?
faq.size.a: macOS DMG ~50 MB · Linux .deb 27 MB · AppImage 43 MB · Windows MSI 43 MB. At idle with one window open, resident memory is ~110 MB; scales linearly per pane. The native next-core engine renders through wgpu; runtime cost is normally dominated by the shell and applications in each pane.
faq.locale.q: Does Unterm detect my system language?
faq.locale.a: Yes. On first launch, Unterm reads the OS locale (defaults on macOS, $LANG on Linux, registry on Windows) and picks the closest of 9 bundled UI languages. You can override per window in Web Settings → Language. Translations live in unterm-services/src/i18n/locales/*.json — patches welcome.
faq.agents_run.q: What stops a rogue agent from running rm -rf on my repo?
faq.agents_run.a: Three gates: (1) MCP server only listens on 127.0.0.1 — no network access. (2) Auth-token gated; the token is in ~/.unterm/instances/<name>.json, an agent without read access to that file can't even connect. (3) First write from a new agent triggers a blocking Allow / Block / Always-allow banner; the audit log records every write attempt with calling agent's identity. You can revoke trust at any time from the Web Settings MCP tab.
faq.script.a: Use unterm-cli: session list, proxy status, theme set midnight, session record start, screenshot. Pass --json to any subcommand for raw JSON-RPC output suitable for shell pipelines and cron jobs.
faq.platform.q: Which platforms ship signed and notarized?
faq.platform.a: macOS: universal arm64 + x86_64 DMG signed with a Developer ID and Apple-notarized + stapled (no Gatekeeper warnings). Linux: .deb for Debian/Ubuntu and AppImage for any distro. Windows: WiX-built MSI installer and portable .zip. All published to GitHub Releases on every minor tag.
faq.opensrc.a: Yes — MIT licensed. The current GUI and terminal runtime use Unterm's native next-core engine, with MCP, Web Settings, recording, i18n, and release tooling in the same repository. Source at github.com/zhitongblog/unterm.
faq.contrib.a: Open an issue or PR on GitHub. The project tracks bugs, feature requests, and discussion in one queue. We bundle accumulated fixes into minor releases — patch-level versions don't trigger CI builds. Documentation lives in-repo at /docs.

whatsnew.mouseux.title: The mouse is a first-class citizen now
whatsnew.mouseux.body: v0.40 is the interaction release. The ⌄ menu is a real mouse menu — icons, hover, shortcuts, instant. Directory jump (Ctrl+Shift+O) opens a Warp-grade palette: recent projects + a type-to-filter subdirectory browser; Enter cds, ⌘Enter opens a new tab there. A collapsible project tree (Ctrl+Shift+B) docks on the left — click to expand, double-click to cd, click a file to insert its quoted path, right-click for copy/reveal/new-tab. Plus quick-action buttons in the tab bar, slimmer edge-flush scrollbars that no longer fight the split divider, cleaner pane-close buttons, a status bar with real hierarchy, and Finder right-click services (“New Unterm Tab Here”) registered on install — the whole surface finally drives as smoothly with a mouse as with a keyboard.
whatsnew.scrollshot.title: Scrolling screenshots — inside and outside the terminal
whatsnew.scrollshot.body: Long screenshots, both directions. Inside: Unterm owns the text model, so it renders your entire scrollback into one tall PNG headlessly — an exact re-render with the same fonts and theme, streaming-encoded so 10,000 rows don’t blow memory, and it works even when the window is occluded. Outside: point at any other app’s window and Unterm scrolls it with synthetic wheel events, then stitches the frames by exact row-hash matching with sticky header/footer detection — a CleanShot-style long shot of Safari, Slack, anything. Both live in the ⌄ menu, in the CLI (unterm-cli screenshot --scrollback / --scroll-app Safari), and as MCP tools (capture.scrollback, capture.window_scroll) so your agents can grab them too.
why.title:
A terminal doesn’t need AI built in.
It needs to be drivable by AI.
why.subtitle: This is the fork between Unterm and Warp — not a feature gap, a direction.
why.lifespan.title: The lifespan mismatch
why.lifespan.body: A terminal is a thirty-year tool; an AI model is a six-month component. Weld the AI into the terminal and the longest-lived tool you own is now defined by its shortest-lived part — when the model ages, the whole terminal ages with it.
why.agents.title: You already have agents
why.agents.body: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Aider — you already run the strongest coding agents there are, and they get better every month. A chat box inside the terminal is just one more copilot to sign into, and it will never be the one you actually prefer.
why.surface.title: What’s missing is grip, not brains
why.surface.body: Agents don’t lack intelligence — they lack hands on the terminal. Unterm makes the terminal an MCP-drivable surface: spawn panes, run commands, read the screen, take scrolling screenshots, change settings, record sessions. An agent uses the terminal the way you do, instead of watching through glass.
why.warp.title: Warp’s answer: put AI inside the terminal
why.warp.b1: AI embedded in the terminal UI, tied to their cloud — login, subscription, quotas
why.warp.b2: Their chosen models, upgraded on their schedule
why.warp.b3: The AI core is closed; your command context flows through their servers
why.unterm.title: Unterm’s answer: hand the terminal to AI
why.unterm.b1: The terminal is an MCP surface — any agent plugs in and drives, today’s or next year’s
why.unterm.b2: You pick the agent and the model; Unterm never locks you in
why.unterm.b3: MIT, fully open source; everything stays on 127.0.0.1 — no login, no subscription, no telemetry
why.closing: You’ll still be using a terminal in thirty years. Nobody knows which AI will be driving it then — which is why the only future-proof terminal is the one built to be driven.
whatsnew.search41.title: Search that feels instant — for you and your agent
whatsnew.search41.body: The in-pane search bar got a full overhaul: it opens instantly, the first keystroke replaces the seeded pattern, match switching and the cursor are finally legible, and in copy mode you can click any match to jump to it. There's a search button in the tab bar now too. The same power went to agents: screen.search learned goto — find a string in the scrollback and jump the viewport straight to it. Plus: a Windows launch freeze (serial proxy probing) is fixed, the MCP stdio bridge now answers introspection even before the GUI starts, and a stall watchdog reports GUI freezes with startup spans.
whatsnew.dirjump42.title: Directory jump that reaches anywhere — deep, fast, CJK-friendly
whatsnew.dirjump42.body: The go-to-directory palette grew real legs. Type a fragment and it matches any depth under your project (bounded recursive scan, noise dirs pruned): term ren lands on …/termwindow/render in one shot. Tab is shell-style completion now — it writes the selected directory into the input with a trailing slash and keeps going, exactly like cd dir<Tab>. Queries starting with / or ~ become live path completion, mounted volumes show up as Finder-style Locations (your second disk is finally reachable by name), and truncated lists say '… N more' instead of pretending to be complete. Plus a fix that mattered: IME-composed text (Chinese/Japanese/Korean input) now reaches modals — previously typed characters leaked into the shell behind the palette, making it look dead.
whatsnew.win43.title: Windows: every drive within reach + no more silent GPU deaths
whatsnew.win43.body: Two Windows-first fixes. Drive letters are separate roots, so the directory-jump palette could never reach D:\ from C:\ — drives now appear as Locations, and queries like D: or d:\code (and UNC \\server\share) flip straight into path completion with backslashes handled. And when no usable OpenGL exists (VMs, RDP sessions, ancient drivers), Unterm used to exit silently on double-click; it now auto-falls back to the WebGpu backend and, if that fails too, says so in a real error dialog instead of vanishing.
cockpit.title: Your terminal now sees the agents running inside it
cockpit.subtitle: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Aider — every pane reports who is working, who is blocked on you, and what they changed. Zero config to start; one command for exact hook-level reporting.
cockpit.state.title: Live state on every tab
cockpit.state.body: Four signal layers — official hooks, title/OSC parsing, process detection, screen heuristics — fold into one state per pane: working (breathing blue), needs you (amber), done, idle. The top bar tallies every window and turns amber the moment anything waits on you.
cockpit.inbox.title: The Agent Inbox
cockpit.inbox.body: <kbd>Ctrl+Shift+A</kbd>: every agent across all windows, sorted waiting-first, with how long it has been stuck and on what. Enter jumps straight to the pane. “Go press y somewhere” is now two keystrokes.
cockpit.fleet.title: Fleet: one task, N agents
cockpit.fleet.body: Race claude × 2 + codex on the same task — each member in its own git worktree and branch beside your repo, its own tab, its own state badge. Your working copy is never touched.
cockpit.review.title: Review: nothing goes untracked
cockpit.review.body: The moment an agent starts working, Unterm checkpoints the repo (a dangling commit — HEAD, index, files untouched). Line-level diffs including agent-created files, squash-merge as staged (the commit stays yours), rollback to any checkpoint, side-by-side member comparison.
cockpit.api.title: Fully scriptable, like everything else
cockpit.api.body: The cockpit itself is MCP + CLI: agent.status, cockpit.inbox, fleet.launch, review.merge… an orchestrating agent can launch fleets and review diffs with no human in the chair. Local-first — none of this touches a cloud.
whatsnew.verify57.title: Fleet verification loop, and a new mark
whatsnew.verify57.body: The fleet closes its own loop. Automatic verification per member — Review infers the right validation command (Cargo / Go / npm / pnpm / yarn / Python / Maven / Gradle / .NET) or runs yours, persists status + log, and gates squash-merge on a passing run (an audited force overrides). Members are ranked by verification and change size; failed ones retry in the same worktree without losing work. Plus review.verify / fleet.retry over MCP + CLI, grouped project navigation with fuzzy search in the sidebar — and the new command-loop brand mark on every surface.
whatsnew.cockpit55.title: Agent Cockpit
whatsnew.cockpit55.body: The terminal now sees the agents inside it: live per-pane state with tab badges and a cross-window tally, the waiting-first Agent Inbox (<kbd>Ctrl+Shift+A</kbd>), fleets running one task across N agents in N isolated worktrees, and a Review page with checkpoints, diffs, rollback, and squash-merge. 12 new MCP methods, 3 new CLI families.
faq.q1: How do I see when Claude Code is waiting for my approval?
faq.a1: Unterm tracks every pane’s agent state. When Claude Code (or Codex, Gemini, Aider) blocks on a confirmation, its tab dot turns amber, the top-bar chip turns amber with a count, and the agent moves to the top of the Agent Inbox (Ctrl+Shift+A) — Enter jumps you straight to that pane. Detection is zero-config for Claude Code and Gemini; “unterm-cli agent enable-hooks” adds exact hook-level reporting.
faq.q2: Can I run multiple Claude Code instances in parallel without them conflicting?
faq.a2: Yes — that is what fleets are for. “unterm-cli fleet launch --agents claude,claude,codex -- task” gives each member its own git worktree and branch beside your repo, so they cannot trample each other or your working copy. Each member gets its own tab with a live state badge, and the Review page compares their results side by side.
faq.q3: How do I review or undo what an AI coding agent changed?
faq.a3: Unterm checkpoints a repo the moment an agent starts working in it — a dangling git commit that never touches HEAD, your index, or your files. The Review page (in Web Settings) shows line-level diffs including files the agent created, lets you squash-merge a take into your repo as staged changes (you make the commit), discard it, or roll the worktree back to any checkpoint.
faq.q4: Does Unterm send my terminal data to the cloud?
faq.a4: No. Unterm has zero telemetry, no account, and no cloud component. The MCP and HTTP servers bind to 127.0.0.1 only, and the entire Agent Cockpit — state detection, fleets, checkpoints, review — runs locally. The only network traffic is whatever your own agents and shells do.
faq.q5: How is Unterm different from Warp?
faq.a5: Warp embeds AI inside the terminal behind a closed cloud orchestrator; external tools cannot drive it. Unterm inverts that: the terminal is an open, MCP-controllable surface that any agent (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Cursor, your own script) drives from outside — and its agent orchestration is local git worktrees and open APIs, not a cloud service. Unterm is MIT-licensed, free forever, with no login.
faq.q6: Which AI coding agents does Unterm support?
faq.a6: The launcher installs and wires Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, and Aider with one click each. The cockpit’s state detection additionally recognizes kimi, trae, and cursor-agent out of the box, and any agent that emits standard terminal signals (titles, OSC 9/777, BEL) gets basic tracking for free. Anything can integrate via “unterm-cli agent signal”.
cmp.c.rmux.title: Unterm vs rmux: the agent's terminal vs the agent's tmux
cmp.c.rmux.desc: rmux is a headless Rust multiplexer with a typed SDK for driving terminal sessions from code. Unterm is a full GPU terminal that agents drive over MCP — and a cockpit for supervising the agents inside it.
cmp.c.rmux.tagline: Both let programs drive a terminal. rmux gives your code a library; Unterm gives your agent a protocol — and gives you a window to watch it all.
cmp.c.rmux.intro: rmux (public preview, v0.2) is a Rust terminal multiplexer in the tmux lineage: a daemon that keeps sessions alive across disconnects, ~90 tmux-compatible commands, native Windows ConPTY, and a typed async SDK with structured pane snapshots and Playwright-style waits. It has no GUI — it is infrastructure for code that uses terminals, and it's genuinely good at that.
cmp.c.rmux.a1: MCP, not an SDK. rmux automation means writing and shipping code against its Rust SDK. Unterm exposes 99 MCP methods — Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, or any MCP client drives the real terminal with zero integration code, auto-discovered on first launch by setup-ai.
cmp.c.rmux.a2: The other direction too. rmux is one-way: code drives terminal. Unterm also watches the agents running inside it — live per-pane state, the waiting-first Inbox, worktree fleets with verification-gated review. The terminal is a cockpit, not just a target.
cmp.c.rmux.a3: A terminal humans use. Unterm is the GPU window you work in all day: right-click copy/paste gesture, identity profiles, 9 UI languages, session recording to redacted markdown. rmux has no rendering surface at all — pairing it with a terminal app is on you.
cmp.c.rmux.win: rmux's session persistence is real tmux-grade: SSH drops and your agent's shell keeps running, reattachable from anywhere. Its typed snapshots and wait_for_text locators are finer-grained than text matching, and a headless daemon fits CI pipelines where no GUI can exist. It's also embeddable in Ratatui apps.
cmp.c.rmux.verdict: Building a system where code owns terminal sessions in CI or on servers? rmux is a strong primitive. Working alongside AI agents at a desk, in a terminal you also live in? That's Unterm — protocol-native for agents, cockpit-native for you.
whatsnew.kernel61.title: Our own kernel: 22ms to a live control surface
whatsnew.kernel61.body: Unterm no longer runs on a WezTerm fork. next-core is a terminal kernel written for this product — parser, screen model, PTY runtime, font stack, and a wgpu renderer — held to a budget of ~12k source lines and 10 direct dependencies. 22ms from launch to a live MCP surface (was 7.1s), idle at 6.6% of a core (was 80%), identical 200k-line throughput. Feature parity with the old kernel was closed item-by-item against a 159-requirement ledger, with platform-native typography: real traffic lights on macOS, pt-accurate sizing, and CJK finally rendered right. Read the story on the blog.
whatsnew.core63.title: Sessions outlive the window — and an install finally contains it
whatsnew.core63.body: unterm-core now owns your sessions: a per-user process that holds shells, scrollback and split layouts, serves the whole MCP surface, and survives the window closing (v0.62). v0.63 is the release the install deserved: the core daemon actually ships in all six packages, the settings page works in Core mode, emoji render for the first time — the bundled face was a COLRv1 font FreeType cannot draw — pause-then-type lag went from 96ms to 8ms, macOS wears the new mark, and Explorer's right-click grows “Open in Unterm tab”.
